newsitem.title: UK: EX-UK TO AMERICAS AIR CARGO STILL HIT BY EXCESS.
newsitem.headline: EX-UK TO AMERICAS AIR CARGO STILL HIT BY EXCESS.

text.p: Excess capacity continued to place a dampener on selective air cargo rates to the Americas from the UK although carriers and forwarders detected a more buoyant undertone to the market, a Reuters survey showed.

Currency factors played an increasing although at times an indirect role, as the strength of the dollar and sterling boosted exports from continental Europe but made cargo rates in European currencies appear too low for international carriers.

Last week Cathay Pacific and Air France said they hoping to increase rates from Europe 10 percent with both the strength of demand and the weakness of European currencies against the dollar cited as factors. Thai Airways on Tuesday said it hoped to introduce very moderate increases in October on its flights to and from Paris citing both good demand and currency factors.

But there were no such clear statements on rates from the UK and the strength of sterling makes it unlikely that ex-UK rates denominated in sterling will have the same excuse to rise as those from continental Europe, carriers and forwarders said.
But this is balanced by the continued high level of UK exports which carriers said had absorbed some or all the extra capacity on routes to the U.S.
Rates most depressed were those on routes where charter companies were trying to generate extra cash flow by filling bellyholds at virtually any price.

But despite this gloomy picture of cut-throat pricing, several carriers said that rates were steady on routes away from the charter market or they had sufficient customer loyalty to carry them through the seasonal capacity surplus in capacity until a balance is restored in the autumn.

The wide ranges of rates quoted on the routes where price cutting was most prevalent plus the impact of seasonal holidays and factory shut-downs - often at slightly different dates in different countries - added to the unclear picture, forwarders said.

Some carriers said there are instances of cargo being flown to Miami at under 30 pence a kg for shipments of over a tonne. Carriers said that on some routes charter holiday operators were foregoing their usual premiums for small shipments, by offering flat rates in a effort to pick-up any business but these carriers were not offering the lowest rates.

"I can't see rates rising until the extra capacity disappears towards the end of September...although the volume of cargo now being flown is consistently buoyant," said Kevin Durnin managing director of Viking Freight Services, a UK cargo general sales agent active in U.S. and South American routes.

Several competitor carriers and forwarders picked out British Airways and Virgin as amongst those offering the most aggressive pricing on the North Atlantic with Virgin in particular offering cutprice rates to Miami.
BA was again quoting low pallet and bin rates but is not interested in loose cargo which it marketed by wholesaler and consolidator Dunwoody Airline Services in which BA has a 40 percent stake.

BA does not want to handle loose cargo itself but it has consistently offered special promotional offers this year for pallets and bins, enabling consolidators to pass on very low rates on sections of BA's global network.
The problem facing U.S. airlines was highlighted by European managing director for cargo John Smith at American Airlines who said that apart from the UK revenues in dollar terms were down.
"Yields from continental Europe are down some 10 percent but are holding up okay from the UK," he added.

But the lower European currencies were ensuring that U.S. import demand is strong and in fact Smith said American were seeing very strong demand both ways. This partially reflected a reduction in capacity this summer owing to a switch in aircraft types.
Cargo volume from the UK where prices of exports are less competitive has been boosted by interline traffic from India, Africa and the Middle east, Smith said.
The net result has been load factors running in the high 80s with no categories of cargo particularly noteworthy.
"It's a bit early yet to be planning rate rises for the autumn but it is nearly inevitable there will be some upward adjustment," he added.
"There is a good volume of business to the U.S. with computer business originating in the U.K. and Ireland a feature," said United Airlines's UK manager Peter Chase.
Chase said United favour a rate increase once a year and that this is most likely in January but added that outside factors such as unforeseen changes in fuel costs can upset such plans.

Last winter all airlines imposed fuel surcharges or upped their cargo rates to compensate for higher fuel charges - later the surcharges were removed or absorbed into an increases in the basic tariff.

Virgin sales manager Justine Delaney said the market has been hit by "massacre rates" to Florida. Carriers said another route hit by very cheap bellyhold holiday charter traffic was from Manchester to Orlando.
Opinions differed more on rates to Washington where Virgin has trucking connections enabling it to offer a good service into the Carolinas and the mid-west.
Confirmation of the high level of business came with Air Canada flying all-time record of 650 tonnes through Heathrow in a single week in July, its UK and Ireland cargo manager Mike Judkins said.

Much of this cargo was destined for the U.S. and much will have originated in continental Europe before being trucked to Heathrow, he added. Produce from the Netherlands, Belgium and Italy helped keep the tonnage high.
Other features were another Rolls-Royce aircraft engine bound for Boeing in Seattle. This went via Toronto where it changed from one Combi to another before being trucked from Vancouver to Seattle.

The production line at Boeing also generated traffic for Rolls Royce jet engines and aircraft line galleys and toilets with GSA's reporting this traffic was carried by Cargolux from Prestwick in Scotland.

UPS entered the fourth day of the strike by Teamster workers in the US with rival express carriers reporting increased numbers of calls. Late on Wednesday both sides agreed to resume negotiations in an effort to settle the strike.

"We are starting to see the increase in UK-U.S. volumes we predicted, somewhat earlier than expected. This can only gain momentum as the week continues if customers find that there is indeed disruption to UPS service schedules," Glyn Jones, DHL UK commercial director said.
The Latin American market had fewer contrasts and descriptions of the activity varied from moderate down to very thin and dull.

As usual high-tech goods were mentioned as featuring amongst cargoes carried. Some carriers reported planes were flying full to and from Brazil with British-made auto sports a feature. A non-event was last month's BA strike where some others carriers had hoped to generate extra business. Although there were a few extra flights, one source who said they expected the phones to be "ringing off the hook" actually saw little new business. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
